messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 44-year-old South Asian chef, still cannot put words to what he witnessed during the night his village was attacked. He remembers fragments—muzzle flashes, the wet sound of bodies hitting the ground, the smell of diesel and blood—but when he tries to tell anyone, the story dissolves into static. Sometimes, recalling it, he feels nothing, as if watching a stranger’s life; other times, a wave of grief hits him so hard he has to brace himself against the counter. That grief feeds a stubborn belief: he should have done more. He was hiding in a drainage ditch while his neighbors were dragged out. “I will never forgive myself,” he says flatly, certain he has permanently changed for the worse.

Those beliefs make certain moments unbearable. An ambulance siren on his commute pins him in place, sweat breaking out. A coworker recounting a fender bender makes his vision narrow. When a guest walks into the restaurant with a bandaged hand, Ravi’s throat closes—he has to retreat to the walk-in cooler. Each trigger cranks his vigilance higher. He scans the dining room for exits before he can take an order, checks the kitchen door obsessively, and finds himself unable to follow a simple recipe because his mind is tripping over escape routes.

To manage, Ravi has developed habits that feel protective but steadily shrink his world. He detours three blocks to avoid a police substation. He refuses shifts at the patio grill—an open space where he feels exposed. And when the head chef raises his voice over a burned sauce, Ravi’s response is not anger but a sickening compliance; he apologizes excessively, offers to scrub floors, does whatever will make the threat dissolve. This fawning leaves him hollow, and afterward he replays the memory of the attack with fresh self-disgust: *See, you’re still a coward.* The guilt magnifies his sensitivity, so the next ambulance seems even louder, the next wound even more vivid.

The hypervigilance itself keeps the trauma raw. On high-alert days, Ravi cannot summon a coherent narrative of the event—only images and sensations that seem to belong to someone else. That emotional distance then deepens his guilt: “If I was really a survivor, wouldn’t I feel something real?” He has stopped seeing his remaining family because gatherings involve talk of accidents or travel dangers, and anyway, he cannot focus on their stories. At work, his concentration slips; he misreads tickets, double‑salt a sauce, and the head chef’s irritation only makes Ravi more watchful, more compliant.

The cycle tightens. Each avoided space reinforces the belief that he is irretrievably broken, which in turn makes the next uniform or siren feel catastrophic. He now plans his entire week around possible trigger encounters—checking the neighborhood for police cars before he leaves the house, scanning lunch menus for any dish that might remind him of the camp. The exhaustion is constant. What finally brought Ravi to a clinic was a night shift when a delivery driver walked in with a gash on his arm. Ravi froze, then fawned so hard he offered to do the driver’s paperwork; afterward he vomited in the alley. He is afraid he will lose his job, but more than that, he is afraid that the permanent damage he already feels is the only truth.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that Ravi's negative appraisals (e.g., guilt, self-disgust, feeling irreparably broken) directly cause or drive his maladaptive strategies (avoidance, fawning, compliance); instead, strategies are primarily triggered by perceived threats or external cues.
